The Arkansas City Traveler contributed to this report.

Extremely dense fog affected Sedgwick County from the late evening on the 26th through the morning on the 27th. Visibilities at times were near zero. Consequently, over 30 accidents occurred across the Wichita Metro between 5 am and noon on the 27th. Several accidents at the Interstate 235 and Broadway interchange forced the closure of Highway 96 at the West Street exit for two hours on the morning of the 27th. Thankfully, no injuries were reported. Property damage amounts are rough estimates. The Wichita Eagle contributed to this report.

During the late morning on the 17th, strong wind gusts out of the west to northwest around 40 mph associated with a passing cold front downed a large bus barn under construction in Russell. The wind gust was measured by ASOS equipment at the Russell Airport. No injuries occurred. Property damage amounts are rough estimates. The Russell County News contributed to this report.

Extreme cold temperatures moved across the county during the overnight hours of February 2nd and early on February 3rd.  Wind chill readings dropped as low as minus 20 degees during the evening of February 2nd, with the low temperatures falling to minus 8 degrees in Coffeyville, Kansas and minus 7 in Independence, Kansas on the morning of February 3rd.||Unfortunately, a 79 year old Coffeyville, Kansas woman died of exposure to the cold, after falling in her backyard while trying to clear snow on the morning of February 2nd.   She apparently was unable to get back up after falling, some 15 feet from her back step and died from exposure to the extreme cold temperatures.  Actual time of death is unknown, but law enforcement authorities say that she had been lying in the location for an extended period of time.

The oppressive heat during the last half of the month led to three heat related fatalities in Hutchinson, Kansas.   The first occurred on July 14th, when a 73 year old man died from heat related causes.   The second occurred on July 16th, when a 63 year old man passed away, and the third occurred on July 20th, when a 76 year old man died of heat stroke.  In all three cases, police reported that the interior temperature inside the homes was 95 degrees.
The oppressive heat led to the death a 65 year old man on July 18th.   The victim was apparently working on a lawn mower when he was overcome by the heat.  He later died from heat related issues.

The searing heat claimed one life, when a 47 year old man was riding his bicycle in the triple digit heat and collapsed on the side of the road near Oxford, Kansas.  He was later pronouced dead from a heat related cardivascular collapse.
The 100 degree heat through the end of the month, led the county to record its third hottest July on record, only surpassed by the heat waves in 1934 and 1980.

During the last half of the month, the city of Wichita, Kansas, recorded 16 out of 17 days above 100 degrees.  The hottest temperatures occurred on July 23rd, when the mercury reached 108 degrees, and July 27th when it reached 111 degrees.  The 111 degree temperature was the second time this month that the temperature had reached that lofty number.  This tied the fourth warmest temperature ever recorded in the city.

In addition to the shed, the east side of the house was a total loss, including a back room and the kitchen. Winds estimated around 70 to 80 mph produced extensive damage to a church in Dubuque in northern Barton county. An outbuilding was damaged, along with the church steeple. Additionally, several windows were broken out of the sacristy, and a wall of a quonset hut was blown away. Just east of Dubuque, the storm produced damage to some homes in the form of broken windows, damaged siding and shredded roofs. Consequently, hail likely occurred at times with the wind, but exact hail size remains unknown. However, reports further northwest in Russell county suggest hail could have been up to golfball size. Some area crops were also heavily damaged, but damage estimates are unknown. Property damage amounts are rough estimates. The Great Bend Tribune was the sole contributor to this report.

A powerful supercell thunderstorm produced extreme straight-line wind damage in the Inman area. Winds estimated up to 90 mph tore a portion of a roof from a residence, and also blew out several windows at that same residence. The city of Wichita, Kansas, recorded three more days of hundred degree heat, with the hottest day being September 1st, when the temperature reached 106.  The significance of this three day heat wave is that it broke the city of Wichita's, record for the number of one hundred degree temperature days in a year at 53.  This broke the previous record of 50 days set in 1936 during the Dust Bowl era.

Winds estimated around 70 mph in conjunction with hail up to baseball size produced damage across Cherryvale. Reported damage included: a power pole snapped, 5-inch diameter tree limbs snapped off, and several windows blown out due to the wind-driven hail. Additionally, various degrees of roof damage and car body damage likely occurred across town. Property damage amounts are rough estimates.

Winds estimated around 70 mph in conjunction with hail ranging from golfball to baseball size produced extensive damage across Cherryvale. The wind-driven hail produced widespread roof, siding, car and window damage across town. City and county officials indicated hundreds of structures sustained some type of damage across town, with property damage estimates between $4 million and $5 million dollars. The Montgomery County Chronicle contributed to this report.

Winds estimated between 90 and 110 mph produced widespread damage across Labette county, including damage to sheds, mobile homes, trees and power lines. The most extensive damage occurred in a three-mile-wide swath roughly 5 to 8 miles south of Parsons, including an overturned and completely destroyed mobile home. County officials estimated that roughly 15 to 18 homes were damaged countywide. Westar reported 25 utility poles downed countywide, resulting in nearly 80 percent of the county without power. Three injuries (direct) were reported across the county, one of which was critical. Property damage amounts are rough estimates. The Wichita Eagle and Parsons Sun contributed to this report.

Some improvement in the drought conditions did occur, as most locations across Central Kansas saw near normal rainfall for the first time in almost nine months which led to the drought dropping to severe limits (D2) by the middle of the month.

Widespread freezing rain caused roads and highways and especially elevated surfaces to become slick and hazardous in and around Russell.  Based on radar trends It would be safe to assume that similar conditions occurred in other parts of the county.

Freezing rain in and around Lyons caused 5 slide-offs that occurred earlier in the event.

Freezing rain was reported in and around Lindsborg where accumulations had begun on trees. That evening, power outages had occurred in parts of Moundridge. Glazing occurred on elevated surfaces, including vehicles in and around McPherson as well as in other parts of the county. Several power lines were downed in McPherson and across the county.
In South Hutchinson, streets started to get slick early in the evening and around mid-late evening all elevated surfaces were glazed. By the morning of the 27th, several intersections were icy.
In Newton, many streets were icy, especially on elevated surfaces.

Freezing rain and sleet were reported, via twitter, at the Kingman Airport. Very late that night, a delayed report was received from the public, via social media, that moderate to heavy freezing rain had occurred at Rago near the intersection of Highways 42 and 14, making streets very slick.

Late in the evening, ice had begun to accumulate, from freezing rain, on vehicles across the county. On the morning of the 27th, broadcast media reported that 1/4 inch of ice had coated Northern Harper County that no doubt made many roads very slick. That afternoon, broadcast media reported that an ice storm had caused widespread power outages in Anthony.

Widespread sleet and freezing rain made travel increasingly dangerous across the county. Very early on the morning of the 28th, law enforcement reported, via social media, that sleet and freezing rain were causing accidents across the Wichita Metro Area. The sleet and freezing rain had also coated trees and vehicles. Early on the morning of the 28th, 0.10 inch of ice had been measured at the forecast office 1 mile west of Eisenhower Airport in the past 18 hours and by that evening, accumulations had reached nearly 1/4 inch in several areas. On the morning of the 29th, an ice storm downed power lines 5 miles southeast of Eisenhower Airport near the South Hydraulic/I-135 interchange, severing power to around 100 residents. An electric utility in Cheney reported that an ice storm downed tree limbs onto power lines that eventually fell. Specifics regarding power outages weren't provided.

The tornado touched down in open country and then moved southeast.  Towards the end of the tornadoes life, a home was hit and completely destroyed with all walls being compromised.  The walls were not adequately secured to the foundation, therefore, a lower rating was provided.  Otherwise, significant tree damage including snapped trunks were widespread along the river valley.  A corn crop was also completely decimated.  The odd track is due to this mesocyclone dissipating and a new one developing to the southeast and it became influenced by the airflow around the new circulation.  This carousal affect also led to such a wide damage path near the end of its life.

A tornado touched down just northwest of the Eureka Country Club and moved southeast across the town.  As the tornado moved through town, it destroyed 31 homes, 23 homes had major damage, and another 32 had minor damage. A total of 152 structures were damaged in some way. The tornado was rated an EF2, due the damage caused across town, with the hardest hit areas, just to the west of the Eureka nursing home.  NO serious injuries or deaths occurred with the tornado.  Eyewitness accounts suggest that residents received ample warning lead time, due to the information being received through the alert function of their mobile devices.

A large grass fire started north of Hutchinson on Sunday March 5th, but was around 90% contained by the early afternoon hours of Monday March 6th. This long track tornado moved in from Pawnee County. Law Enforcement reported the tornado just south of the county line near Pawnee Rock and then followed it as it moved to the NE.  The tornado moved through the west side of Pawnee Rock causing sporadic EF1 and isolated EF2 damage to several homes and one school type facility.  The tornado continued to move to the NNE causing EF2 damage to a couple of homes on West Barton County Road.  One residence was a mobile home that lost the far east side of the structure and all roofing material.  One injury was noted at that location as they did not seek shelter.  The home just to the west lost the east half of structure with the occupants seeking refuge in the basement.  Of note, a Ford F-150 was thrown or rolled approximately 75 to hundred yards away from its original location.  Further to the NE, the tornado strengthened considerably as noted by complete destruction of an 1890 farm house.  With the age of the home and no anchoring being present due to the structure resting on cinder blocks along with a lack of debarking, a higher rating could not be justified though the amount of devastation to the structure itself pointed towards a possible higher rating.  Three occupants sought refuge in the basement and were unharmed.  The next door neighbor's home was also considerably damaged with all of the structure being demolished except for one corner section. The tornado then continued to the NE over open country damaging trees and power lines along the way before dissipating NW of Hoisington. A total of 44 parcels were affected. Ten homes were deemed total losses.  The estimated property value losses were estimated at $658,000.

Areas of light freezing drizzle and flurries likely contributed to a fatal car accident (indirect) around 1:50 a.m. in Hesston on February 21st. A 24-year-old Goessel man was killed in the 500 block of South Ridge Road in Hesston when his vehicle slid off the road and struck a tree. He was pronounced dead at the scene. Ice and snow accumulations were very minor, but enough to create slick conditions. Information courtesy The Hutchinson News.

A wintry mix of snow, sleet and freezing rain during the afternoon hours of February 23rd eventually changed over to all snow during the evening hours, and accumulated up to 2 inches across Allen County before ending around 11 p.m. Associated slick road conditions led to a fatal car accident (indirect) on Highway 54 near Iola around 8:30 p.m. The 32-year-old Iola woman was killed when she lost control of her vehicle. Information courtesy The Wichita Eagle.

Areas of light freezing rain, sleet and snow likely contributed to an injury accident (indirect) around 3:50 p.m. on Interstate 135 near the Assaria/Smolan exit. The 25-year-old Lincoln, Nebraska woman was traveling northbound on the interstate when she lost control and entered the center median, after a tractor-trailer passed her. The area received about 2 inches of snow, along with light freezing rain and sleet accumulations. Information courtesy The Salina Journal.

Areas of light freezing rain, sleet and snow likely contributed to two injury accidents (indirect) across Barton County during the afternoon hours of February 23rd. A 44-year-old Hoisington woman was injured when her car slid into the ditch on K-4 Highway near NW 120 Ave around 2:45 p.m. The other injury accident occurred around 1:15 p.m. near Antelope north of Great Bend when a 31-year-old Hoisington woman's car slid off Washington Street and rolled onto its side. Snow accumulated about 4 inches, while ice and sleet accumulations remained light. Information courtesy The Great Bend Tribune.

Areas of light freezing rain, sleet and snow likely contributed to an injury car accident (indirect) just north of Ellsworth on K-156 shortly before 4 p.m. on February 23rd. The pickup driver, a 47-year-old Manhattan woman, slid across the center line and collided with a semi-trailer, injuring herself and two passengers: an 18-year-old Manhattan woman, and an 18-year-old Hays man. Four to five inches of snow accumulated across the area, with ice and sleet accumulations remaining light. Information courtesy The Great Bend Tribune.

An intense bow echo moved across northern Butler county producing widespread wind damage from the Potwin area through Cassoday. Slow moving thunderstorms produced very heavy rainfall amounts across primarily the northern half of Marion County from the mid-morning into the afternoon hours of April 23rd. Rainfall amounts exceeded 6 inches for some locations, with rainfall rates around 2 inches per hour at times. Hillsboro reported 4.96 inches, and Marion reported 5.36 inches. Widespread flooding occurred across mainly the northern half of Marion County, which prompted numerous road closures. Some roads were covered with nearly 6 feet of water. As a result, several roads and culverts sustained some form of damage, along with some county bridges. Especially hard hit was the town of Durham, when the North Cottonwood River backed up due to a 3.5-foot rise in the Marion Reservoir, flooding portions of the town with up to 18 inches of water. Some homes and businesses received flood damage. Some farmers from around the area stated they had never seen the Cottonwood River that high, although an older gentleman stated he had seen the river higher twice before, most notably in 1951. High water finally subsided by the morning hours of April 24th. Information courtesy of the Marion County Record and the Hillsboro Free Press.

The QLCS tornado touched down just outside of Turon, KS, and moved to the NNE across town.  The bulk of the damage was limited to trees as the tornado strength at the surface appeared to be much lower than that at tree top level.  A few homes and buildings were damaged as trees fell onto many roofs and some sheet metal was peeled off of a barn.  Some playground equipment was also blown over in the park close to where the tornado lifted. Winds were estimated to be around 80 mph with this tornado.
Lightning struck the water tower in Sylvan Grove which led to the issuance of a boil water advisory for the town. Time is estimated based on radar data.

Widespread non-thunderstorm winds wreaked havoc across the county.  Sustained wind speeds routinely ranged between 40 to 50 mph with gusts reaching well into the 70 mph range.  One measured gust of 100 mph was noted at the peak.  These wind speeds caused considerable damage countywide to structures, routinely caused reduced visibilities due to blowing dust, temporarily closed Interstate 70, blew down a significant number of power lines, and fueled the wildfires that were ignited.
